claims.text: A Cr coating containing approximately 5 at.% Hf will form a stable Hf-rich interphase at the Cr–Zr interface.
The Hf-rich interphase will retard Cr–Zr interdiffusion during high-temperature steam exposure.
Adding approximately 5 at.% Hf will preserve the coating's protective function during normal subcritical-water operation.
Normal subcritical-water operation is represented by a temperature around 300°C.
Accident-relevant high-temperature steam conditions are represented by temperatures above 800°C for transient exposures of approximately 1–2 hours.
The interfacial Hf-rich phase will be continuous.
Hf dopants will preferentially segregate during coating deposition.
Hf dopants will preferentially segregate during subsequent thermal exposure.
Segregated Hf will form a thermally stable interfacial phase.
The Hf-rich interphase will act as a diffusion barrier that reduces the migration of both Cr and Zr atoms.
Reduced Cr and Zr migration will mitigate premature coating failure caused by elevated-temperature interdiffusion.
Approximately 5 at.% Hf will not compromise protective oxide-layer formation at lower temperatures.
After high-temperature steam exposure, the Hf-doped coating will have significantly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion than an unmodified Cr coating.
After high-temperature steam exposure, the Hf-doped coating will retain a more distinct coating–substrate boundary than an unmodified Cr coating.
The Hf-doped coating will preserve corrosion resistance during subsequent operation in subcritical water.
An unmodified elemental Cr coating undergoes premature interdiffusion and coating failure under accident-relevant high-temperature conditions.
The proposed protection is expected to extend from hundreds of hours near 300°C to 1–2-hour high-temperature steam transients above 800°C.
